questions.stem: A 35 year old mother brings her 7 year old son, who started vomiting and having watery diarrhoea 12 hours ago. Two classmates were off school with the same illness this week. He is drinking sips, alert and passing urine. His temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. She asks how long it is likely to last.
questions.q: Which is the most likely duration of his illness?
questions.e: Viral gastroenteritis such as norovirus typically lasts 1 to 3 days.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely duration of his illness? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A short outbreak illness in a school: **viral gastroenteritis**.

elim: Too short; that is closer to the course of a preformed toxin.
Suggests a parasite such as Giardia, or another cause.
Chronic diarrhoea needs investigation.
Longer than typical for norovirus; persistent illness needs review.

steps.x: **E. About 1 to 3 days.** Viral gastroenteritis is short: 1 to 3 days.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman in a care home has had norovirus for 2 days, with vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She takes furosemide and ramipril. She is now drowsy with a dry tongue. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 90 to 210 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
questions.e: Dehydration is the main risk of viral gastroenteritis, especially in older people on diuretics and ACE inhibitors, causing hypotension and acute kidney injury.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Dry, hypotensive, AKI, on drugs that worsen fluid loss.

elim: Norovirus does not invade the bloodstream.
Not suggested; no diabetes treatment.
Not a complication of viral gastroenteritis.
A complication of colitis such as C. difficile or UC.

steps.x: **B. Dehydration.** Main risk of viral gastroenteritis: dehydration.

questions.stem: Twenty pupils on a residential school trip develop sudden profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea over 2 days. The first cases began about 30 hours after arriving at the hostel. Several teachers become ill a day later. Nobody has blood in their stool and most recover within 2 days.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Outbreaks in closed settings with profuse vomiting and diarrhoea 12–48 hours after exposure, lasting 1–3 days, are classic norovirus.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Several teachers become ill a day later
steps.x: **Closed setting**, onset **12–48 h**, spread to staff, quick recovery.

elim: Milder, longer diarrhoea in young children.
Bloody diarrhoea after 2–4 days, without person-to-person spread through staff.
Mainly affects children under 5.
Onset within 1–6 hours of food and does not spread person to person.

steps.x: **C. Norovirus.** Closed-setting outbreak of vomiting = norovirus.

questions.stem: A 27 year old staff nurse has had vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 20 hours. She works on a ward where six patients have had similar symptoms this week. She has not eaten out or travelled. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of her infection?
questions.e: Close contact in an outbreak setting is the most important risk factor for viral gastroenteritis; contaminated food and water are less common sources.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely source of her infection? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: six patients have had similar symptoms
steps.x: She works in an **outbreak setting**.

elim: She has not eaten out.
Would point to C. difficile, not an outbreak.
She has not travelled.
Linked to Campylobacter and Salmonella.

steps.x: **A. Close contact with affected patients.** Viral gastroenteritis: biggest risk factor is close contact in an outbreak.

questions.stem: A health visitor explains rotavirus gastroenteritis to new parents at a baby clinic. They ask at what age their baby would be most likely to get severe rotavirus infection if not vaccinated.
questions.q: Which age range is most at risk?
questions.e: Rotavirus is most common in children under 5, with a peak at 6 to 24 months.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which age range is most at risk? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: most likely to get severe rotavirus infection
steps.x: Rotavirus is a disease of **young children**.

elim: Maternal antibodies offer some protection, and it is not the peak.
Older children have usually had rotavirus already.
Not a peak age.
A risk group for norovirus outbreaks in care homes, not the rotavirus peak.

steps.x: **C. 6 to 24 months.** Rotavirus peaks at 6 to 24 months.

questions.stem: A 2 year old girl has had loose watery stools 4 times a day for 9 days. She has had a low-grade fever of 37.9°C, occasional vomiting and both her eyes are red and sticky. She is drinking well and alert. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and capillary refill time 1 second.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Adenovirus 40 and 41 cause milder, subacute diarrhoea in children with low-grade fever and vomiting, sometimes with URTI or conjunctivitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Milder, **longer** illness with **conjunctivitis** in a toddler.

elim: Bloody diarrhoea with abdominal pain.
Follows travel; no conjunctivitis.
Profuse vomiting, lasting only 1–3 days.
High fever and profuse diarrhoea; no conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **A. Adenovirus serotypes 40 and 41.** Subacute diarrhoea + low fever + conjunctivitis/URTI in a child = adenovirus 40/41.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days. He is lethargic with sunken eyes. His pulse rate is 160 bpm, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and BP 84/50 mmHg. His hands are cool.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most strongly indicate clinical shock?
questions.e: In children, a prolonged capillary refill time of over 2 to 3 seconds suggests clinical shock rather than dehydration alone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which additional finding would most strongly indicate clinical shock? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Already tachycardic and cool. Which sign tips **dehydration** into **shock**?

elim: A sign of dehydration, not shock.
A sign of dehydration, not shock.
A sign of dehydration, not shock.
Mild fever does not indicate shock.

steps.x: **B. Capillary refill time of 4 seconds.** Shock: CRT >2–3 seconds (NICE diarrhoea and vomiting in children).

questions.stem: A nursery reports an outbreak of diarrhoea among its under-2 room. A 13 month old boy has had watery diarrhoea 10 times a day and vomiting for 2 days, with a temperature of 39.4°C. He has not had his routine immunisations. His pulse rate is 150 bpm and capillary refill time 2 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Rotavirus causes acute watery diarrhoea with high fever and vomiting in children under 5, sometimes needing admission; vaccination reduces it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**High fever**, profuse diarrhoea, toddler, **unvaccinated**.

elim: Milder diarrhoea with low-grade fever.
Follows antibiotics.
Mainly closed-setting outbreaks in adults; less often this high a fever.
Systemic fever after travel to an endemic area.

steps.x: **D. Rotavirus.** High fever + profuse watery diarrhoea in an unvaccinated toddler = rotavirus.

questions.stem: A family of four returns from a hotel holiday in Spain. Within a day, all of them develop vomiting and watery diarrhoea, one after another. None has blood in the stool. Other guests at the hotel had been unwell. The father's temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea spreading through a family and hotel is viral gastroenteritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Rapid **person-to-person** spread with vomiting and diarrhoea.

elim: Bloody diarrhoea with abdominal pain and a prodrome.
Weeks of bloating and diarrhoea.
Chronic, not an acute family outbreak.
Prolonged stepwise fever with constipation first.

steps.x: **E. Viral gastroenteritis.** Acute D&V spreading through a group = viral gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is alert but has a dry mouth, sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and capillary refill time 2 seconds. Her hands are warm.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate assessment of her fluid status?
questions.e: Dry mouth, sunken eyes, reduced turgor and tachycardia with a normal CRT and warm hands is clinical dehydration without shock.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most accurate assessment of her fluid status? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Dehydration signs, but **CRT normal**, **warm** and **alert**.

elim: Needs signs such as CRT over 2–3 seconds, cold peripheries or reduced consciousness.
She has lost fluid.
Dry mouth, sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor are dehydration.
No signs of shock or sepsis.

steps.x: **A. Clinical dehydration without shock.** Dehydration vs shock: CRT >2–3 s, cold hands and drowsiness mean shock.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man is admitted with a hip fracture. Two days later the patient in the next bed develops profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea and norovirus is confirmed. The man's daughter asks how soon her father might become unwell if he has caught it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely incubation period?
questions.e: Norovirus causes acute watery diarrhoea and profuse vomiting 12 to 48 hours after exposure, lasting 1 to 3 days; hospitals are a classic outbreak setting.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely incubation period? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **norovirus** contact in a **hospital**: how long until symptoms?

elim: The incubation of Staphylococcus aureus preformed toxin.
Too long for any acute viral gastroenteritis.
Too long for norovirus.
Closer to typhoid.

steps.x: **B. 12 to 48 hours.** Norovirus: onset 12–48 hours after exposure, lasts 1–3 days.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has had vomiting and loose stools for 18 hours. His sister had the same illness last week. He is alert, drinking and passing urine. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and capillary refill time 1 second. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Viral gastroenteritis is largely a clinical diagnosis; most cases need no investigation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: His sister had the same illness
steps.x: A well child with a typical short illness and a sick contact.

elim: Not needed with a soft abdomen.
Not indicated in an afebrile child with D&V.
Only if severe, immunocompromised or persistent.
Only if severely dehydrated or unwell.

steps.x: **C. Clinical assessment alone.** Viral gastroenteritis: clinical diagnosis, no tests if well.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has had watery diarrhoea for 12 days after a norovirus outbreak at his care home. Other residents recovered within 3 days. He is tired but drinking. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 120/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Persistent, severe or immunocompromised cases need a stool sample and U&Es to assess dehydration.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Persistent** beyond the usual 1–3 days.

elim: Does not identify the cause.
Not first line.
Not first line without signs of an acute abdomen.
Persistent symptoms need testing.

steps.x: **E. Stool sample and U&Es.** Investigate if severe, immunocompromised or persistent: stool sample and U&Es.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has had profuse vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days during a norovirus outbreak at her office. She now feels faint on standing and has passed very little urine today. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 98/62 mmHg lying, 84/50 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: In severe viral gastroenteritis, U&Es assess dehydration, kidney function and electrolytes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Severe dehydration** with postural drop and oliguria.

elim: Does not guide rehydration.
She is not septic.
Not indicated in acute gastroenteritis.
Do not assess dehydration.

steps.x: **E. Urea and electrolytes.** Severe cases: U&Es to assess dehydration.

questions.stem: On an elderly care ward, five patients develop sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea within 48 hours. Two are frail and becoming dehydrated. The infection control team wants to confirm the cause of the outbreak.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Outbreaks in hospitals and severe cases warrant stool samples (norovirus PCR) to confirm the cause, with U&Es for dehydrated patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confirm the cause of the outbreak
steps.x: A **closed-setting outbreak**: likely norovirus, confirm from stool.

elim: Viral gastroenteritis is not bacteraemic.
Not relevant to diarrhoea.
Invasive and unhelpful.
Used for respiratory viruses.

steps.x: **D. Stool samples from affected patients.** Hospital outbreak: send stool samples.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 24 hours. He tries to drink but vomits every time. He is alert with a dry mouth. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg and capillary refill time 2 seconds. He is not dizzy on standing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral rehydration solution with an antiemetic
questions.e: Mild to moderate dehydration is treated with ORS first line; antiemetics can help symptom control so that oral fluids stay down.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild-moderate dehydration, but **vomiting** is stopping oral fluids.

elim: He is not severely dehydrated or shocked.
Does not replace fluid.
Antibiotics do not treat viral infection.
For C. difficile.

steps.x: **D. Oral rehydration solution with an antiemetic.** ORS first line; antiemetics for symptom control.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has had watery diarrhoea and vomiting for 1 day after her grandchildren were ill with the same. She is thirsty with a slightly dry mouth. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. She is managing to keep down small drinks.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Rehydration, not antimicrobials, is the mainstay; ORS is first line for mild to moderate dehydration.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild dehydration, **keeping fluids down**, viral contact.

elim: Not needed in mild dehydration with oral intake.
Antibiotics have no role in viral gastroenteritis.
For Giardia or C. difficile.
Not needed in mild typical illness.

steps.x: **D. Oral rehydration solution.** Viral gastroenteritis: ORS first line.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy weighing 20 kg has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 3 days. He is drowsy with mottled cold hands. His pulse rate is 170 bpm, capillary refill time 5 seconds and BP 78/42 mmHg. IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid?
questions.e: Shock needs a 20 mL/kg bolus of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline): 20 x 20 kg = 400 mL.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Shocked** child: give a **20 mL/kg** crystalloid bolus.

elim: Only 5 mL/kg; too little for shock.
Glucose is not used for resuscitation, and the volume is wrong.
Not the first-line resuscitation fluid.
Too slow in shock.

steps.x: **D. 400 mL 0.9% sodium chloride bolus.** Shock in gastroenteritis: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus.

questions.stem: A GP sees a 2 year old girl with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. She is very drowsy and floppy, with cold peripheries and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Her pulse rate is 175 bpm. She has refused all drinks today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Send a stool sample and review results
Urgent hospital referral for IV fluids
questions.e: Severe dehydration or shock needs hospital referral for IV fluids.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Signs of **shock** in a child.

elim: Delays treatment of shock.
Do not treat viral gastroenteritis or shock.
Not safe in shock.
Does not treat a shocked child.

steps.x: **E. Urgent hospital referral for IV fluids.** Severe dehydration or shock: hospital for IV fluids.

questions.stem: A 38 year old care home kitchen worker has had norovirus with vomiting and diarrhoea. Her symptoms stopped this morning and she feels well. She asks when she can return to work.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Return once she has a negative stool sample
Return today if she uses alcohol gel
Return today if she wears gloves
Stay off work until 48 hours after symptoms stop
questions.e: Infection control prevents spread: hand hygiene and exclusion until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting, especially for food handlers and care workers.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **food handler** in a care home who could spread norovirus.

elim: Clearance stool tests are not routinely needed.
Alcohol gel does not reliably kill norovirus.
She remains infectious for a time after symptoms stop.
Longer than needed.

steps.x: **E. Stay off work until 48 hours after symptoms stop.** Infection control: 48 hours symptom-free before returning; soap and water.

questions.stem: During a norovirus outbreak on a hospital ward, staff have been cleaning their hands with alcohol gel between patients, but cases keep rising. The infection control nurse reviews hand hygiene.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change in practice?
o: Hand washing with soap and water
questions.e: Norovirus is a non-enveloped RNA virus resistant to alcohol-based sanitisers, so soap-and-water hand washing and strict isolation control outbreaks.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate change in practice? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Alcohol gel is **failing** against norovirus.

elim: Antibiotics do not act on viruses.
Gloves do not replace hand washing.
Not the main route of spread.
Norovirus is resistant to alcohol.

steps.x: **C. Hand washing with soap and water.** Norovirus: soap and water, not alcohol gel.

questions.stem: The father of a 3 year old with viral gastroenteritis asks for antibiotics. The child has had watery diarrhoea and vomiting for 1 day without blood. She is alert and drinking. Her pulse rate is 115 bpm and capillary refill time 1 second.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that rehydration, not antibiotics, is the treatment
Send stool for culture before deciding
questions.e: Fluid loss is secretory and osmotic, not from mucosal invasion, so supportive rehydration with ORS is the mainstay, not antimicrobials.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate response? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A well child with typical **viral** illness.

elim: Antibiotics do not treat viral gastroenteritis.
Not used in young children.
For Giardia or C. difficile.
Not needed in a well child.

steps.x: **A. Explain that rehydration, not antibiotics, is the treatment.** Rehydration is the mainstay; antibiotics have no role.

questions.stem: A 16 month old boy is recovering from rotavirus gastroenteritis. His mother notices that his diarrhoea worsens and he has bloating every time he drinks cow's milk. Stool pH is low and stool tests positive for reducing substances.
questions.q: Which enzyme activity is most likely reduced?
questions.e: Rotavirus destroys mature enterocytes at the villous tips, reducing disaccharidase (lactase) activity and causing an osmotic, secondary lactose intolerance-type diarrhoea.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which enzyme activity is most likely reduced? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diarrhoea after **milk** with sugar in the stool, after rotavirus.

elim: Pancreatic protease; not affected.
Pancreatic enzyme; would cause steatorrhoea.
Not affected by rotavirus.
Pancreatic protease; not affected.

steps.x: **B. Lactase.** Rotavirus: villous tip damage, reduced disaccharidases, secondary lactose intolerance.

questions.stem: A 10 month old girl has rotavirus gastroenteritis. Small bowel histology from a research study of similar infants shows loss of mature cells at the villous tips with shortened villi. Her watery stools improve when she is fasted.
questions.q: Which type of diarrhoea is this most likely to be?
questions.e: Rotavirus destroys enterocytes at the villous tips, so unabsorbed sugars draw water into the lumen: an osmotic diarrhoea that improves with fasting.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of diarrhoea is this most likely to be? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diarrhoea that **stops with fasting** is osmotic.

elim: Seen with mucosal invasion and blood, such as Shigella.
Seen in IBD with blood and pus.
As in hyperthyroidism or IBS.
Persists despite fasting, as in cholera.

steps.x: **D. Osmotic.** Rotavirus diarrhoea is mainly osmotic.

questions.stem: A medical student asks why patients with norovirus gastroenteritis receive fluids rather than antimicrobials, when patients with typhoid receive antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Fluid loss is secretory and osmotic without mucosal invasion
Norovirus is a bacterium resistant to antibiotics
Norovirus is resistant to all antivirals because it is enveloped
questions.e: Viral gastroenteritis causes secretory and osmotic fluid loss without mucosal invasion, so supportive rehydration is the mainstay, not antimicrobials.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the best explanation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Compare an **invasive** systemic bacterium with a self-limiting gut virus.

elim: Norovirus is a virus.
Norovirus is non-enveloped, and this is not the reason.
It stays in the gut.
Rehydration replaces losses; the immune system clears the virus.

steps.x: **A. Fluid loss is secretory and osmotic without mucosal invasion.** Rehydration, not antimicrobials, because fluid loss is secretory/osmotic.

questions.stem: A paediatric registrar compares admissions to her hospital for severe gastroenteritis in children under 5, before and after a routine oral vaccine was introduced to the UK childhood immunisation schedule in 2013. Admissions fell sharply after its introduction.
questions.q: Which vaccine most likely explains the change?
questions.e: Rotavirus vaccine is part of the UK childhood immunisation schedule and has substantially reduced hospital admissions for severe paediatric gastroenteritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which vaccine most likely explains the change? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
An **oral** routine childhood vaccine reducing **paediatric gastroenteritis** admissions.

elim: Not part of the routine UK schedule.
Prevents measles, mumps and rubella.
Not available on the UK schedule.
For travellers, not routine childhood.

steps.x: **D. Rotavirus vaccine.** Rotavirus vaccine (UK schedule) cut paediatric gastroenteritis admissions.
